tagline: Mountains, horses and high summer pastures
overview:
Kyrgyzstan is a small, mountainous country in Central Asia where mountains cover more than 90 percent of the land. Landlocked between Kazakhstan, China, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, it is about the size of South Dakota. The Tian Shan, whose name means heavenly mountains, fills most of the country with peaks, glaciers and high valleys. Bishkek, the capital, lies on a northern plain beneath a wall of snowy summits.

About 7 million people live in Kyrgyzstan. Kyrgyz, a Turkic language, is the state language, and Russian has official status and is widely used in the cities. Kyrgyzstan is a republic and has changed governments through popular protests several times since independence. Farming and herding support many families, and in summer whole households move up to the jailoo, high mountain pastures, living in yurts while their animals graze. Gold mining and money sent home by relatives working abroad are major sources of income.
landAndNature: Glaciers and snowfields blanket the high Tian Shan, where Jengish Chokusu reaches 7,439 meters on the border with China. Meltwater from these mountains feeds rivers that supply much of Central Asia. Lake Issyk-Kul, ringed by peaks at about 1,600 meters, is one of the largest and deepest mountain lakes in the world and never freezes, thanks to slightly salty water and great depth. The walnut forests near Arslanbob are the biggest natural walnut woods on the planet. Snow leopards, ibex, marmots and golden eagles live on the high slopes, and in spring the valleys turn red and purple with wild tulips and poppies.
peopleAndCulture: Kyrgyz culture grew out of a nomadic life on horseback, and horses still matter enormously. Kok-boru, a fierce team game played on horseback with a heavy goat carcass instead of a ball, is the national sport. Families drink kumis, fermented mare's milk, and eat beshbarmak, boiled meat served over wide noodles. Yurts, round felt tents, are raised for summer pastures and celebrations, and the pattern at the center of a yurt roof appears on the national flag. Shyrdak felt rugs are stitched in bold curling designs. The Manas, an oral epic longer than the Iliad and Odyssey together, is recited from memory by trained storytellers.
history: Nomadic peoples herded across these valleys for thousands of years, and Silk Road caravans crossed the high passes between China and the west. The Kyrgyz are thought to have moved south from the Yenisei region of Siberia over many centuries. Mongol armies arrived in the 1200s, and the Khanate of Kokand ruled parts of the land before the Russian Empire took control in the 1800s. Under Soviet rule from the 1920s, herders were forced onto collective farms, schools and hospitals were built, and Kyrgyz was written in Cyrillic letters. Kyrgyzstan became independent in 1991. Protests removed presidents in 2005, 2010 and 2020, and ethnic violence struck the south in 2010.
funFacts: Mountains cover more than 90 percent of Kyrgyzstan, and much of the country lies above 1,500 meters.
The Epic of Manas, recited from memory by specialists, is one of the longest poems ever composed.
The design in the middle of the Kyrgyz flag is the roof opening of a yurt, seen from inside looking up.
Lake Issyk-Kul never freezes despite its mountain setting, and its name means warm lake in Kyrgyz.
In kok-boru, the national sport, riders gallop while trying to heave a goat carcass into the opposing team's goal.
